L79: # Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
L80: 
L81: Andres Saurez Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Daejeon 34051, South Korea    Yousung Lee Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Daejeon 34051, South Korea    Dongsoo Har Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Daejeon 34051, South Korea Correspondence to: dshar@kaist.ac.kr
L82: ###### Abstract
L83: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders consistently recover meaningful structure from transformer representations—yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, nonlinear systems? We show this is not merely an empirical regularity but a consequence of architectural necessity: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces (attention OV circuits, unembedding matrices), and any semantic feature decoded through such an interface must occupy a context-invariant linear subspace.
L84: We formalize this as the Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem and derive the Self-Reference Property: tokens directly provide the geometric direction for their associated features, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic structure without labeled data or learned probes. Empirical validation in eight classification tasks and four model families confirms the alignment between class tokens and semantically related instances.
L85: Our framework provides a principled architectural explanation for why linear interpretability methods work, unifying linear probes and sparse autoencoders.
L86: ###### Keywords:
L87: 
L88: Machine Learning, ICML
L89: ## 1 Introduction
L90: Linear structure has become a central organizing principle in modern interpretability for transformers (cite67†Vaswani et al., 2017 ). Linear probes recover semantic attributes from hidden states (cite68†Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; cite69†Belinkov, 2022 ), sparse autoencoders (SAE) identify interpretable feature directions (cite70†Bricken et al., 2023 ; cite71†Cunningham et al., 2023 ), and single-vector activation steering reliably modifies model behavior (cite72†Turner et al., 2023 ; cite73†Zou et al., 2023 ).
L91: Across a wide range of methods and objectives, simple linear operations repeatedly succeed at isolating meaningful internal structures.
L92: cite74†Image: Refer to caption Figure 1: Context-invariant directional representation. The explicit token “France” provides a reference vector for this direction (self-reference), while contextual mentions such as “I went to Paris” and “I visited Marseille” share the same invariant direction.
L93: Yet this success raises a fundamental theoretical puzzle. Transformers are deep, highly nonlinear systems trained with simple objectives but exhibiting complex emergent behavior. Why, then, should their internal representations admit such simple and reliable linear access to semantic information? Recent theoretical work suggests that linear representations can emerge from the next-token prediction objective together with the implicit bias of gradient descent (cite75†Jiang et al., 2024 ).
L94: We provide a complementary explanation: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces—most notably the attention OV circuit and the unembedding matrix—and any semantic feature read out through such an interface must reside in a context-invariant linear subspace. While optimization determines how representations are learned, architecture constrains what form they must take.
L95: We formalize this claim in our central theoretical result, the Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem: whenever a semantic feature is decoded through a linear interface, its representation must lie in an invariant subspace shared across all contexts expressing that feature. This provides a principled explanation for why linear probes, sparse autoencoders, and direction-based steering are able to recover stable semantic structure.
L96: Crucially, if such an invariant subspace exists, how can we identify its direction in practice? A key derivation from it is the Self-Reference Property: tokens and expressions that encode a feature directly provide its geometric direction in activation space.
L97: For example, the token “France” does not merely instantiate the France concept, but serves as a reference vector for locating that concept in any representation, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic directions without labeled data or learned probes.
L98: We empirically validate these predictions across eight semantic classification tasks spanning taxonomic, affective, stylistic, linguistic, and descriptive domains, and across multiple model families (LLaMA3-8B  (cite76†Grattafiori and others, 2024 ), Mistral-7B (cite77†Jiang et al., 2023 ), GPT2-Small (cite78†Radford et al., 2019 ), LLaMA3.2-3B (cite79†Meta AI, 2024 )). Our results reveal consistent evidence of context-invariant directional structure, supporting the generality of our theory.
L99: In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) We provide a principled architectural explanation for why linear interpretability methods succeed in transformers, showing that linear structure arises as a necessary consequence of linear communication interfaces.
L100: (2) We introduce the Self-Reference Property, establishing that tokens directly define directions for their associated features—this enables zero-shot identification of semantic directions and yields an unsupervised probe that classifies instances using only class token geometry.
L101: (3) We demonstrate convergent evidence for directional invariance: sparse autoencoders trained without class supervision recover features that align with class token directions, validating that both methods access the same underlying structure.
L102: ## 2 Related Work
L103: ### 2.1 Mechanistic Interpretability
L104: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain model behavior by identifying internal features, circuits, and causal mechanisms inside neural networks rather than relying solely on input–output correlations (cite80†Elhage et al., 2021 ; cite81†Nanda et al., 2023 ).
L105: Transformer models contain identifiable computational substructures implementing specific behaviors, and targeted interventions on internal activations can causally alter model outputs (cite82†Meng et al., 2022 ; cite83†Wang et al., 2022 ; cite72†Turner et al., 2023 ; cite73†Zou et al., 2023 ). Our work connects this literature to representation geometry by providing a theoretical account of the linear, context-invariant feature structure that underlies many of these observations.
L106: ### 2.2 Linear Representation
L107: Semantic attributes can often be captured by low-dimensional linear structure in representation spaces, dating back to linear regularities in word embeddings (cite84†Mikolov et al., 2013 ; cite85†Pennington et al., 2014 ). In modern LMs, linear structure is operationalized as measurement (linear probes that extract a property) and as intervention (steering representations along a direction) (cite86†Kim et al., 2018 ; cite87†Ravfogel et al., 2020 ). cite88†Park et al.
L108: (2024) formalize these intuitions, clarifying what “linear representation” means and how measurement and intervention relate geometrically. Most closely related, cite75†Jiang et al. (2024) explain linear representations through the next-token prediction objective and implicit bias of gradient descent, whereas we give an architectural account of why linear, context-invariant directions are necessary in models with linear communication interfaces.
L109: ### 2.3 Linear Probes
L110: Linear probes test what information is present in hidden states (cite68†Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; cite89†Hewitt and Manning, 2019 ; cite90†Tenney et al., 2019 ). A range of successful techniques instantiate this idea: the logit lens decodes intermediate representations using the unembedding matrix, revealing that hidden states already resemble next-token distributions (cite91†nostalgebraist, 2020 ), and the tuned lens extends this with layer-specific affine transformations (cite92†Belrose et al., 2023 ).
L111: Relatedly, linear directions identified by probes have been used not only for measurement but also for intervention, enabling activation steering of hidden states (cite93†Li et al., 2023 ; cite94†Rimsky and others, 2024 ). Recent evaluations further show that sparse autoencoder latents do not consistently outperform simple linear baselines on probing tasks (cite95†Kantamneni et al., 2025 ). Together, these results highlight the surprising effectiveness of linear readouts and interventions across diverse settings.
L112: However, they remain largely descriptive and do not explain why such linear decodability should arise in deep nonlinear models. Our theory addresses this gap.
L113: ## 3 Theoretical Framework: Identity-Projection
L114: 
L115: We develop a geometric framework explaining how transformers encode semantic features. Our central result establishes that features communicated through linear interfaces must occupy invariant subspaces—a structural consequence of architecture—and we show that optimization dynamics favor low-dimensional realizations.
L116: 
L117: ### 3.1 Preliminaries and Assumptions
L118: 
L119: We consider decoder-only transformers with the following properties:
L120: ###### Assumption 3.1 (Architectural Requirements).
L121: 
L122: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with $L$ layers and hidden dimension $d$. We assume:
L123: 
L124:   1. 1.
L125: 
L126: Additive Residual Stream. The residual stream updates additively: $\mathbf{r}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}+\Delta^{(\ell)}$, where $\Delta^{(\ell)}$ is the output of layer $\ell$.
L127: 
L128:   2. 2.
L129: 
L130: Linear Communication Interfaces. The OV circuit in attention ($W_{O}W_{V}$) and the unembedding layer ($W_{U}$) act as linear maps on the residual stream.
L131: 
L132:   3. 3.
L133: Shared Parameters. The same parameters are applied across all token positions; optimization occurs over parameters shared across contexts.
L134: 
L135:   4. 4.
L136: 
L137: Linear Output Layer. Token logits are computed via linear projection: $\text{logits}=W_{U}\mathbf{r}^{(L)}$.
L138: 
L139: These assumptions hold for standard transformer architectures including GPT-2, LLaMA, and similar models.
L140: ### 3.2 Formal Definitions
L141: 
L142: ###### Definition 3.2 (Context).
L143: 
L144: A context $c=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};i)$ consists of an input token sequence and a position of interest $i$. We write $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(c)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for the hidden state at layer $\ell$ and position $i$ in context $c$.
L145: ###### Definition 3.3 (Semantic Feature).
L146: 
L147: A semantic feature is a function $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{Y}$ mapping contexts to a value space $\mathcal{Y}$. For classification tasks, $\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{K}\}$ is finite.
L148: ###### Definition 3.4 (Communicable Feature).
L149: 
L150: A semantic feature $f$ is communicable if it satisfies both:
L151: 
L152:   1. 1.
L153: 
L154: Multi-context: There exist distinct contexts $c_{1},c_{2}$ with $f(c_{1})=f(c_{2})$.
L155: 
L156:   2. 2.
L157: 
L158: Linear decodability: The feature value is recoverable through a linear interface. For unembedding:
L159: 
L160:  | $$\exists\,\boldsymbol{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}:\quad\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}W_{U}\mathbf{h}(c)=g(f(c))\quad\forall c\in\mathcal{C}$$  |  | (1)
L161: 
L162: for some function $g:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$.
L163: The multi-context requirement captures that meaningful features appear across different surface realizations (e.g., “France” and “the country of the Eiffel Tower” both express the France feature). Linear decodability captures that the feature must be extractable by downstream linear operations.
L164: ###### Definition 3.5 (Invariant Subspace).
L165: 
L166: A communicable feature $f$ exhibits contextual invariance if there exists a subspace $\mathcal{S}_{f}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$, determined by $f$ and model parameters alone, such that for all contexts $c$ expressing $f$, the $f$-relevant information in $\mathbf{h}(c)$ lies entirely within $\mathcal{S}_{f}$.
L167: ###### Definition 3.6 (Directional Invariance).
L168: 
L169: A communicable feature $f$ exhibits directional invariance if it exhibits contextual invariance with $\dim(\mathcal{S}_{f})=1$, i.e., $\mathcal{S}_{f}=\text{span}(\{\mathbf{d}_{f}\})$ for some direction $\mathbf{d}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$.
L170: cite96†Image: Refer to caption Figure 2: Linear readout layers constrain representation geometry. We train a transformer on modular division with an MLP classification head instead of linear unembedding. (Left) When the model finds a non-Fourier solution, embeddings lack circular structure and linear probes fail ($\sim$20% accuracy). (Right) When the model discovers Fourier structure, linear probes succeed.
L171: Across random seeds, linear probe accuracy correlates with the Fourier representations emerges, but are not required by MLP heads. Linear readout interfaces would necessitate such directional structure.
L172: ### 3.3 Main Theoretical Results
L173: 
L174: Our first result establishes that invariant subspace structure is necessary for any feature communicated through linear interfaces.
L175: ###### Theorem 3.7 (Invariant Subspace Necessity).
L176: 
L177: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer satisfying Assumption cite97†3.1 , and let $f$ be a communicable feature decoded through a linear interface $W$. Then there exists a context-invariant subspace $\mathcal{S}_{f}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ such that the $f$-relevant component of $\mathbf{h}(c)$ lies in $\mathcal{S}_{f}$ for all contexts $c$ expressing $f$.
L178: ###### Proof sketch.
L179: 
L180: By linear decodability, the $f$-relevant output is $o_{f}(c)=\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)$ for some $\mathbf{w}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Contexts requiring identical outputs differ only in $\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\perp}$, so $f$-relevant information lies in a subspace determined by $\mathbf{w}_{f}$ alone—independent of context. Full proof in Appendix cite38†A . ∎
L181: ### 3.4 Capacity Constraints Force Factorized Representations
L182: 
L183: The unembedding matrix $W_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}$ maps hidden states to logits over $|\mathcal{V}|$ tokens. With $|\mathcal{V}|\gg d$, tokens cannot occupy orthogonal directions—they must share structure.
L184: ###### Proposition 3.8 (Capacity Constraint Implies Feature Sharing).
L185: 
L186: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with vocabulary $|\mathcal{V}|$ and hidden dimension $d$, where $|\mathcal{V}|\gg d$. If (i) token logits are computed via linear readout $\textup{logit}_{t}=\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)$, (ii) each context activates a sparse subset of features, and (iii) multiple tokens share semantic attributes, then the optimal representation factorizes as:
L187:  | $$\mathbf{w}_{t}=\sum_{f\in F_{t}}\alpha_{t,f}\,\mathbf{d}_{f}$$  |  | (2)
L188: 
L189: where $\{\mathbf{d}_{f}\}$ are shared feature directions with $|F|\ll|\mathcal{V}|$.
L190: ###### Proof sketch.
L191: With $|\mathcal{V}|\gg d$, tokens must share directions. Sharing incurs interference only when tokens co-occur; for sparse features, this cost is minimal. Factorization achieves $|F|$ dimensions plus sparse interference, versus the infeasible $|\mathcal{V}|$ dimensions for unique encodings.
L192: Under factorization, $\textup{logit}_{t}=\sum_{f\in F_{t}}\alpha_{t,f}(\mathbf{d}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c))$, so each factor $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ must be linearly decodable and context-invariant—satisfying the conditions of Theorem cite98†3.7 . Full proof in Appendix cite41†B . ∎
L193: ###### Remark 3.9 (Implicit Classification Revisited).
L194: 
L195: From this view, predicting a token is implicit classification: the model checks “does this context encode the factor combination for token $t$?” Each factor $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ partitions contexts into those expressing $f$ versus those that do not. The compression pressure ensures factors are reusable across tokens, maximizing the number of features that can coexist in the representation.
L196: This compression pressure aligns with the information bottleneck principle (cite99†Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015 ): representations must discard context-specific details while preserving task-relevant features, favoring low-dimensional factorized encodings.
L197: ###### Corollary 3.10 (Directional Decomposition).
L198: 
L199: If feature $f$ exhibits directional invariance with direction $\mathbf{d}_{f}$, then for all contexts $c$ expressing $f$:
L200: 
L201:  | $$\mathbf{h}(c)=\alpha_{f}(c)\cdot\mathbf{d}_{f}+\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)$$  |  | (3)
L202: 
L203: where $\alpha_{f}(c)\in\mathbb{R}$ is a context-dependent magnitude and $\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)\perp\mathbf{d}_{f}$ captures the rest of the features.
L204: This decomposition is central: the direction $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ is invariant across contexts, while the magnitude $\alpha_{f}(c)$ varies. Linear interfaces preserve this structure:
L205: 
L206:  | $$W(\alpha\cdot\mathbf{d}_{f})=\alpha\cdot(W\mathbf{d}_{f})$$  |  | (4)
L207:

L216: ### 3.5 The Identity-Projection Operator
L217: 
L218: We now introduce the operator that enables practical applications.
L219: ###### Definition 3.11 (Identity-Projection Operator).
L220: 
L221: For a context $c$ and feature $f$ with invariant direction $\mathbf{d}_{f}$, the Identity-Projection is:
L222: 
L223:  | $$\mathcal{I}_{f}(c)\triangleq\mathbf{h}(c)^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{f}$$  |  | (5)
L224: 
L225: where $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{f}=\mathbf{d}_{f}/\|\mathbf{d}_{f}\|$ is the unit direction.
L226: The Identity-Projection operator focuses on feature $f$ within the representation $\mathbf{h}(c)$. By architectural necessity (Theorem cite98†3.7 ), $f$ flows through $\mathbf{h}(c)$ along direction $\mathbf{d}_{f}$; projecting onto this direction extracts the feature’s signal from the superposition of all features present.
L227: ###### Proposition 3.12 (Feature Operations).
L228: 
L229: If feature $f$ satisfies directional invariance, then:
L230: 
L231:   1. (i)
L232: 
L233: Detection: $\mathcal{I}_{f}(c)>\tau$ indicates $f\in c$ for an appropriate threshold $\tau$
L234: 
L235:   2. (ii)
L236: 
L237: Measurement: $|\mathcal{I}_{f}(c)|$ quantifies feature strength
L238: ###### Proof.
L239: 
L240: From the decomposition (cite104†3 ):
L241: 
L242:  | $$\mathcal{I}_{f}(c)=\alpha_{f}(c)\|\mathbf{d}_{f}\|+\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{f}$$  |  | (6)
L243: 
L244: When features are approximately orthogonal ($\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{f}\approx 0$), we have $\mathcal{I}_{f}(c)\propto\alpha_{f}(c)$, and the operations follow from linearity. ∎
L245: ### 3.6 Linear Readouts Constrain Representation Geometry
L246: 
L247: To validate Theorem cite98†3.7 , we compare representation geometry under linear versus nonlinear readout layers. If linear interfaces necessitate invariant subspace structure, then replacing the linear head with an MLP should relax this constraint.
L248: Setup. Prior work on grokking (cite105†Power et al., 2022 ) shows that transformers learning modular arithmetic develop Fourier representations—embeddings arranged in a circle where addition becomes rotation. cite75†Jiang et al. (2024) argue this linear structure emerges from training dynamics (gradient descent + cross-entropy) regardless of architecture. We test an alternative hypothesis: linear structure emerges because linear readout layers require it.
L249: Experiment. We train a 2-layer transformer on modular division ($p=97$) with an MLP classification head instead of the standard linear unembedding. A separate linear probe is trained on the same hidden states (with gradients detached). The MLP head achieves $\sim$95% validation accuracy, but the linear probe fails ($\sim$20%). Fourier analysis (Fig. cite106†2 ) confirms the embeddings lack circular structure—PCA shows scattered points rather than an ordered circle.
L250: Key finding. Across random seeds, some runs do develop (see Fig.cite106†2 ) Fourier structure—and in exactly those runs, the linear probe also succeeds. This correlation demonstrates that Fourier representations are not inevitable: they emerge when the model happens to find that solution, but nonlinear readouts permit alternatives. Linear interfaces constrain representations to be directional; nonlinear interfaces permit but do not require such structure.
L251: ### 3.7 The Self-Reference Property
L252: 
L253: A key question remains: how do we obtain $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ without supervision? Our central insight is that tokens themselves provide these directions.
L254: ###### Theorem 3.13 (Self-Reference Property).
L255: 
L256: Let $t$ be a token with associated semantic feature $f_{t}$. If $f_{t}$ is communicated through linear interfaces, then $t$’s representation provides the invariant direction for $f_{t}$:
L257: 
L258:  | $$\mathbf{h}_{t}\propto\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}$$  |
L259: 
L260: where $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ is obtained by passing token $t$ through the model.
L261: ###### Proof sketch.
L262: 
L263: By Theorem cite98†3.7 , $f_{t}$ occupies an invariant subspace $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}$. Under directional invariance (Proposition cite107†B.2 ), $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}=\text{span}(\{\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}\})$. Since $t$ canonically expresses $f_{t}$, its representation must lie in $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}$, hence $\mathbf{h}_{t}=\lambda_{t}\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}$ for some scalar $\lambda_{t}$. L264: ###### Remark 3.14 (Tokens Provide Directions).
L265: 
L266: The Self-Reference Property has a simple practical implication: tokens tell you where to look. To find the “France” feature in any representation, obtain the direction from the token “France” and project onto it. The feature is there—flowing through invariant directions by architectural necessity—and focusing on the right direction reveals it.
L267: ###### Remark 3.15 (Why “Identity-Projection”).
L268: 
L269: The framework’s name reflects this self-referential structure: projecting onto the direction provided by token $t$ focuses on $t$’s identity—the features that define $t$. The token serves as its own reference point.
L270: ### 3.8 Empirical Validation of the Self-Reference Property
L271: 
L272: Theorem cite108†3.13 predicts that token representations align with the invariant directions of their associated features. We test this by comparing each class token’s hidden state against the mean instance vector for each class, computed across attention heads.
L273: Specifically, for each attention head and class $k$, we compute the cosine similarity between the class token direction $\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}$ and the mean instance direction $\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{k}$ for the same class (within-class) versus other classes (between-class). If tokens provide feature directions as predicted, within-class similarity should consistently exceed between-class similarity.
L274: Figure cite109†3 confirms this prediction: across 89.6%-98.6% of attention heads, the class token aligns more strongly with its own class instances than with any other class. This pattern validates the Self-Reference Property—tokens encode the same directional features present in contexts expressing those features, enabling zero-shot extraction of semantic directions.
L275: ## 4 Methods for Extracting Directions
L276: 
L277: The Self-Reference Property (Theorem cite108†3.13 ) has a practical consequence: since tokens provide feature directions and communicable features are linear (Theorem cite98†3.7 ), a classifier built on token directions should generalize to instances it was never trained on.
L278: A probe anchored to the “France” or “South Korea” direction (which we call a class token or class prompt) should correctly classify implicit prompts like “the country of the Eiffel Tower” or “the country of the Han River” (which we call an instance prompt) —not because it memorized this mapping, but because the France feature flows through the same invariant direction regardless of the surface form.
L279: We compare three approaches that leverage this insight, each with different tradeoffs between simplicity and expressiveness. All three methods perform classification using the Identity-Projection operator (Definition cite110†3.11 ), projecting the query onto normalized class directions. They differ only in how representations are transformed before projection. All probes operate on individual attention-head outputs, and we evaluate each attention head independently.
L280: #### Zero-Shot Probe.
L281: 
L282: The most direct instantiation of the Self-Reference Property is to use class-token hidden states themselves as class directions, without any training. To isolate class-specific components, we mean-center the token representations to remove features shared across all classes (e.g., “being a country”):
L283:  | $$\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{k}=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}\|},\quad\bar{\mathbf{h}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbf{h}_{t_{j}}.$$  |  | (7)
L284: 
L285: Classification is then performed by projecting instance representations onto these normalized directions. This procedure requires no training data.
L286: #### Unsupervised Probe.
L287: 
L288: We train a lightweight linear probe that aligns instance activations with class-token directions using only class tokens. Given an instance activation $\mathbf{h}$ and class-token prototypes $\{\mathbf{c}_{k}\}$ from the same head, the probe learns a transformation $W$ by minimizing the contrastive objective
L289: 
L290:  | $$\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{k}\log\frac{\exp((W\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})^{\top}\mathbf{c}_{k}/\tau)}{\sum_{j}\exp((W\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})^{\top}\mathbf{c}_{j}/\tau)}.$$  |  | (8)
L291: Crucially, $W$ is trained using only class tokens—no instance labels are used. The Self-Reference Property predicts that this transformation should generalize: if tokens and instances share invariant directions, orthogonalizing tokens automatically orthogonalizes instances. Table cite111†2 confirms this—the unsupervised probe matches or exceeds zero-shot performance despite never observing instances during training.
